The weighted sum reconstructs total duration, 2,000, and would answer a total-resource-use question. Without division by 101 it does not compute the requested per-execution mean.
MAX returns 1,000, the largest supplied interval average. It is useful for identifying the largest aggregate interval mean, not the mean across all executions or a maximum individual execution.

The numerator reconstructs represented total duration, 2000, but has not normalized by 101 executions. It would answer a total-duration question, not the requested mean. The unit's weighted-mean expression includes the missing denominator explicitly.

MAX(avg_duration) returns 1000, the larger aggregate row mean. It can rank the worst interval mean, not the combined per-execution mean; it also must not be described as the maximum individual execution duration.

claims.summary: Retrying only the failed statement would omit the first UPDATE because the entire victim transaction was rolled back. A statement-only retry can be meaningful for a different operation whose unit of work is that single statement.
COMMIT finalizes a surviving transaction; error 1205 has already rolled back this victim transaction. It cannot preserve the original transaction's first update.
Waiting for a lock can resume an ordinarily blocked transaction before victim selection. Once 1205 is returned, the old transaction does not survive to resume.

A fresh transaction must repeat both updates after the safe bounded delay. The explicit absence of external effects and safe whole-operation retry premise are essential; arbitrary business operations are not automatically retryable.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Deadlock detection and Handle deadlocks state that error 1205 follows rollback of the victim transaction; all its work is undone. Handle with TRY...CATCH permits catching the error, and retry guidance recommends a brief randomized pause. Ordinary blocking instead waits on a surviving transaction.

choiceReviews.rationale: The victim is the entire explicit transaction, not just its second UPDATE. Retrying only that statement loses the rolled-back first UPDATE and no longer repeats the stated atomic operation. A one-statement unit of work would be a different case.

Error 1205 reports rollback of the original victim transaction, so its changes cannot be committed afterward. A CATCH block can still run, but that control-flow continuation does not mean the original transaction survived.

Waiting may allow an ordinarily blocked, still-live transaction to resume after its blocker completes. Here victim selection and error 1205 have already ended the original transaction. A delay is useful before a new attempt, not to resume the rolled-back attempt.

Starting a new transaction and repeating both UPDATEs reconstructs the complete atomic operation after rollback. The bounded retry, randomized pause and absence of external effects satisfy the recovery assumptions; this does not license unbounded retries or repeating a non-idempotent external action.

review.verificationNotes: Independent answer: d. No executable retry snippet is authored here, and no SQL was executed. Approval does not endorse an unconditional second ROLLBACK of an already rolled-back transaction. The module summary directly links the exact Deadlocks guide, with complete course/path ancestry inspected. Intermediate troubleshooting is appropriate for interpreting a two-statement atomic boundary. Its longer correct option expresses that boundary without persuasive qualifiers. The baseline/live record has this same canonical ID and fact; the separate SNAPSHOT candidate adds stale read-derived calculation semantics, and the sleeping-blocker candidate has no victim/error-1205 event. review.confidenceReason: High confidence from the product guide's explicit transaction-wide rollback and randomized retry guidance. Safe whole-operation retry and absence of external effects are supplied, so neither statement-only recovery nor survival of the old transaction remains defensible.

Business Critical supplies local SSD storage and a readable replica for demanding OLTP. It also has a documented 4-TB data limit, so those advantages do not meet the 12-TB requirement.

Serverless can fit intermittent demand, but changing compute tier does not remove General Purpose's storage boundary. This workload is also steady rather than the stated intermittent serverless use case.
Hyperscale supports storage well beyond 12 TB and named replicas for read scale-out. Provisioned compute matches the stipulated steady resource use without relying on Preview high-vCore sizes.

Steady usage favors provisioned compute; serverless is not being asserted technically incapable of every steady workload.

The captured Hyperscale limit accommodates 12 TB, and the product section explicitly provides named replicas for read scale-out. Provisioned compute matches steady demand. The answer requires neither Preview 160/192-vCore sizes nor a promise about price, latency or replica freshness.

claims.summary: MAXDOP constrains query parallelism and can be relevant to CPU/thread contention. It does not select compiled stubs instead of full first-use ad hoc plans.
The configuration unit documents a small compiled plan stub on first execution and a full cached plan on reuse. That specifically addresses the supplied single-use plan-cache footprint.
Compatibility level enables version-specific optimizer behavior. It is relevant to testing newer optimizer features, not the named control for retaining stubs for first-use ad hoc statements.
Automatic plan correction addresses regressions between alternative plans for a query. It is useful for that scenario, not the accumulation of many distinct statements executed once.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Reduce plan cache bloat explicitly documents ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET OPTIMIZE_FOR_AD_HOC_WORKLOADS = ON and first-use compiled plan stubs. Separate sections assign MAXDOP to parallelism, compatibility level to optimizer behavior, and FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN to regression correction; none is the documented stub-retention control.

choiceReviews.rationale: MAXDOP controls parallel execution and can help a demonstrated parallelism/thread-contention problem. Setting it to one does not instruct the cache to retain only first-use ad hoc stubs. The supplied diagnosis is storage consumed by many distinct single-use plans, not parallel execution.

The retrieved Azure SQL Database unit explicitly provides this database-scoped switch and says first execution retains a compiled plan stub instead of a full cached plan. That targets first-use cache footprint; it does not eliminate first-execution compilation or promise indefinite residency of every important plan.

Compatibility level selects version-dependent optimizer behavior and should be evaluated against a baseline when changed. Level 170 is not the named setting for first-use ad hoc stub retention. It may be relevant when adopting an optimizer feature, not as a substitute for the cache-policy control asked here.

FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN addresses a query's regression to a worse plan by restoring a prior good plan. Thousands of distinct statements executed only once are a cache-footprint problem, not a prior-plan regression case. Automatic plan correction is real but does not select first-use stubs.

review.verificationNotes: Independent answer: b. Actual cited text demonstrates database-scoped Azure SQL Database syntax, not a server-level sp_configure prescription. The negative-wording warning is a useful exclusion of parallelism/plan forcing, not a negative-selection task; 'Their' and 'that goal' unambiguously refer to the plans and cache footprint. All four settings are real alternatives for other diagnoses. Intermediate is credible for targeted configuration selection. Distinct from capacity sizing and retained Query Store history.
